tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: If you heat ice, it melts.
If the library opens early, Maya will finish her essay before lunch.
If it rains tomorrow, we will cancels the picnic.
If Leo studies tonight, he passes the quiz for certain next week.
If the oven is ready, Sara will bakes the muffins.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Zero conditional: present simple in both clauses for a general scientific fact that always holds.

Tip: Rules and natural facts → present + present, not will.

TRUE — First conditional: a real future plan takes present simple after if and will + base verb in the result.

Tip: Real near-future plans → if + present, main clause will + V1.

FALSE — After will the verb must stay bare: will cancel, not will cancels.

Tip: Modals never take a third-person -s on the following verb.

FALSE — A real future result needs will pass (or similar), not a bare present "passes" when you mean next week's outcome.

Tip: Open future results after a real condition usually take will, not plain present.

FALSE — Will takes the base form bake, not bakes.

Tip: Scan will + verb: if you see an -s, the line is broken.
tasks.solution_overview: Warm up on zero versus first: facts keep present + present; real plans keep present + will. Three lines fail on form — will + -s, and a bare present where a future result needs will.

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: If plants get no water, they die.
If Nora books the tickets today, we will sit together on the train.
If the bus is late, Tom will misses his lecture.
If you mix red and blue, you will get purple every time as a law of nature.
If the gym opens at six, Ana will train before work.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Zero conditional correctly states a general consequence with present simple on both sides.

Tip: Habitual or scientific truths prefer zero, not will.

TRUE — First conditional correctly links a real booking decision to a future seating plan.

Tip: Present in the if-clause; will in the result for open futures.

FALSE — Will misses is ungrammatical; use will miss.

Tip: After will, always use the bare infinitive.

FALSE — A timeless colour fact belongs in zero conditional (you get purple), not first with will.

Tip: If the result is always true, drop will and keep present + present.

TRUE — Clean first conditional for a real morning plan.

Tip: Real timetable + real intention → present + will.
tasks.solution_overview: Separate always-true rules (zero) from open future plans (first). Reject will + -s, and reject will when the sentence is really stating a permanent fact.

tasks.title: Task 3
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: If I were you, I would take the earlier train.
If the weather were better, we would cycle to the lake.
If she would have more free time, she would join the choir.
If Dan lived closer, he would walk to campus every day.
If I was the team captain tomorrow in this hypothetical, I would change the formation.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Second conditional with formal were after if I, plus would + base verb for unreal advice.

Tip: Exams prefer If I were … would … for hypothetical roles.

TRUE — Past simple/were in the if-clause plus would marks an unreal present wish about the weather.

Tip: Unreal now → if + past, result would + V1.

FALSE — Do not put would in the if-clause; use If she had more free time…

Tip: Keep would in the result only; the if-clause wants past simple.

TRUE — Standard second conditional for a counterfactual present about distance and commuting.

Tip: Past simple + would is the default unreal-present frame.

FALSE — Careful exam English prefers were for unreal be after if, not was, especially in formal true/false items.

Tip: Hypothetical be → were is the safe exam choice.
tasks.solution_overview: These lines introduce unreal present (second conditional). Watch for would inside the if-clause and prefer were over was in careful hypothetical be.

tasks.title: Task 4
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Unless it rains, the match will go ahead.
As long as you water the herbs, they will stay fresh.
Unless you will hurry, we will miss the opening credits.
If only I knew her phone number now.
I wish I can speak Italian fluently this semester.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Unless (= if not) + present simple pairs cleanly with will for a real future sports plan.

Tip: Treat unless like if not: present in the condition, will in the result.

TRUE — As long as (= provided that) takes present simple for a real ongoing condition, then will in the result.

Tip: As long as / provided that → present + will for open conditions.

FALSE — After unless, avoid will; use present: Unless you hurry…

Tip: Unless / if / as long as rarely take will in the condition clause.

TRUE — If only + past simple correctly wishes about an unreal present lack of knowledge.

Tip: Present regrets with wish / if only → past simple.

FALSE — Wish about present ability needs past form: I wish I could speak…, not can.

Tip: After wish, shift the tense back one step from reality.
tasks.solution_overview: Meet unless, as long as, and wish / if only at entry level. Keep will out of the condition clause, and shift tenses back after wish for present unreal situations.

tasks.title: Task 5
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: If the cinema had more evening slots, we would go more often.
If I had known about the sale, I would have bought the jacket.
If they would practise every day, they would improve faster.
Unless Mia finishes her lab report, she will not watch the film.
As long as the neighbours keep quiet, I can revise until midnight.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Second conditional for an unreal present about the cinema timetable.

Tip: Unreal present → past simple + would.

TRUE — Third conditional: past perfect in the if-clause and would have + past participle for a missed past opportunity.

Tip: Unreal past → if + had + V3, result would have + V3.

FALSE — Would does not belong in the if-clause; use If they practised…

Tip: Ban would from the condition; leave it for the result.

TRUE — Unless + present correctly sets a real study condition before a future plan.

Tip: Unless + present + will / will not is exam-safe for real futures.

TRUE — As long as + present states a real proviso that enables present ability.

Tip: As long as can support present results (can / may) as well as will.
tasks.solution_overview: Blend second, third, unless, and as long as. The only clear fail is would inside the if-clause; everything else keeps the condition form clean.

tasks.title: Task 6
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: If the ferry had left on time, we would have reached the island before dusk.
Had she set an alarm, she would not have overslept.
If Ben had trained harder, he will have won the race.
I wish I had packed an umbrella yesterday.
If only the Wi-Fi worked in this café right now.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Classic third conditional for a missed travel outcome in the past.

Tip: Past unreal → had + V3 / would have + V3.

TRUE — Inverted third conditional (Had she set…) correctly replaces If she had set…

Tip: Had + subject + V3 is a formal shortcut for if + past perfect.

FALSE — The result must stay in the unreal past: would have won, not will have won.

Tip: Third conditional results use would have, never will have.

TRUE — Wish + past perfect correctly regrets a past packing choice.

Tip: Past regrets after wish / if only → past perfect.

TRUE — If only + past simple correctly wishes about an unreal present problem.

Tip: Present inconvenience → past simple after if only.
tasks.solution_overview: Focus on unreal past: third conditional, Had-inversion, and wish / if only. Reject will have where would have is required.

tasks.title: Task 7
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: If you don't water the tomatoes, they will wilt.
Unless you don't water the tomatoes, they will wilt.
As long as students submit drafts on Friday, the tutor will give feedback on Monday.
I wish the neighbours would stop drilling at dawn.
If only she will listen to the podcast before the seminar.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — First conditional with a negative if-clause correctly predicts a real future result.

Tip: If + present (affirmative or negative) + will is fine for open futures.

FALSE — Unless already means if not, so Unless you don't creates a messy double negative; use Unless you water… or If you don't…

Tip: Avoid stacking unless with another negative.

TRUE — As long as + present correctly sets a real academic condition for a future result.

Tip: Provided / as long as behave like if for real conditions.

TRUE — Wish + would correctly complains about someone else's annoying present habit.

Tip: Wish + would = desire for a change in someone else's behaviour.

FALSE — If only for a present/future wish needs past or would, not will: If only she would listen… / If only she listened…

Tip: After if only, do not keep ordinary will.
tasks.solution_overview: Watch polarity with unless, keep as long as in present for real plans, and use wish / if only + would for behaviour you want to change — not will.

tasks.title: Task 8
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: If the trail were less muddy, we would hike further.
If prices fall next month, more families will switch to seasonal produce.
If I would be taller, I would reach the top shelf easily.
Unless the museum closes early, we will see the sculpture wing.
I wish I were better at mental arithmetic.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Second conditional with were for an unreal present outdoor scenario.

Tip: Unreal be → were is preferred in careful English.

TRUE — First conditional: a real possible price change pairs with will switch. One everyday-economy line is fine among lifestyle topics.

Tip: Real future possibility → present + will.

FALSE — Never write If I would be; use If I were / If I was (exam: were).

Tip: Would stays out of the if-clause in standard conditionals.

TRUE — Unless + present + will correctly frames a real museum visit plan.

Tip: Unless = if not; keep present in the condition.

TRUE — Wish + were correctly marks an unreal present ability.

Tip: Wish I were is the formal pattern for present counterfactuals with be.
tasks.solution_overview: Consolidate second conditional, unless, wish + were, and one real first-conditional lifestyle/price line. The trap is If I would be.

tasks.title: Task 9
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: If she had taken the earlier bus, she would be at the theatre now.
If he were more organised, he would have handed in the portfolio last Friday.
If they had left earlier, they would arrive yesterday evening.
If I had more patience as a child, I would have learned piano sooner.
If you heated the soup now, it would taste better.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Mixed conditional: past unreal cause (had taken) with present result (would be).

Tip: Past perfect in if + would + V1 = past cause, present effect.

TRUE — Mixed conditional: unreal present character (were) with past result (would have handed).

Tip: If + past / were + would have + V3 = present unreal trait, past consequence.

FALSE — A finished past result needs would have arrived, not would arrive, after a past perfect condition.

Tip: Past condition + past result → third, not first-looking would + V1 with yesterday.

FALSE — A childhood past state needs past perfect: If I had had more patience as a child…

Tip: Pure past regrets need had + past participle in the if-clause.

TRUE — Second conditional can use past simple heated for an unreal/unlikely present suggestion.

Tip: Soft hypothetical now → past + would.
highlights: If I had more patience as a child
tasks.solution_overview: Enter mixed conditionals: match the time of the cause to the time of the result. Reject would + V1 with clear past time markers, and reject weak past-perfect gaps in childhood regrets.

tasks.title: Task 10
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: As long as you will follow the recipe, the cake will rise.
Provided that the pool is open, we will swim after class.
I wish I didn't have to revise tonight.
If only they hadn't cancelled the outdoor concert last Saturday.
Unless she had missed the call, she would answer it now.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — As long as takes present for real conditions: As long as you follow…, not will follow.

Tip: Keep will out of as long as / provided that clauses.

TRUE — Provided that + present + will is a clean real-future proviso.

Tip: Provided that ≈ if / as long as for open conditions.

TRUE — Wish + past simple correctly regrets a present obligation.

Tip: Present annoyance after wish → past simple (didn't have to).

TRUE — If only + past perfect correctly regrets a finished past cancellation.

Tip: Closed past regrets → past perfect after if only / wish.

FALSE — The timelines clash: a past-perfect unless-clause wants a past result (would have answered), or rephrase as Unless she misses… she will answer / If she hadn't missed… she would answer now with matching mixed forms carefully.

Tip: Align condition time and result time; don't paste past perfect onto a plain would + V1 present without a clear mixed pattern.
tasks.solution_overview: Tighten connectors (as long as / provided that) and wish / if only tense shifts. Reject will after as long as and messy unless + past perfect with a simple present result.

tasks.title: Task 11
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: If the tutor explained the theorem more slowly, more students would have passed last week's test.
If the tutor had explained the theorem more slowly, more students would pass the resit next month.
If the tutor had explained the theorem more slowly last term, more students would understand it now.
Had the trail been clearer, we would not have got lost.
If it weren't for the fog, we could see the harbour lights.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Mixed conditional: unreal present teaching style (explained) with a finished past result (would have passed).

Tip: If + past + would have + V3 = present unreal trait, past consequence.

FALSE — A finished past explanation (had explained) does not pair cleanly with a plain future would pass next month; use would have passed for a past test, or If she explained… would pass for unreal present/future.

Tip: Align the time of the condition with the time of the result.

TRUE — Mixed: past unreal teaching (had explained) with present result (would understand now).

Tip: Had + V3 / would + V1 = past cause, present effect.

TRUE — Inverted third conditional correctly reports a past hiking mishap avoided in an alternate past.

Tip: Had + subject + been / V3 replaces If + past perfect.

TRUE — If it weren't for + noun correctly introduces an unreal present obstacle, with could in the result.

Tip: If it weren't for X = without X (unreal present).
tasks.solution_overview: Drill mixed timelines with a lifestyle pricing example, plus inversion and If it weren't for. Only the clearly time-aligned mixed line and the two standard patterns survive.

tasks.title: Task 12
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: I wish you wouldn't leave your shoes in the hallway.
I wish you don't leave your shoes in the hallway.
If only the semester break were longer.
If water freezes, it will expands.
If water freezes, it expands.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Wish + would correctly asks for a change in habitual annoying behaviour.

Tip: Wish + would = stop doing that / please change.

FALSE — Wish does not take present simple like a command; use wouldn't leave or didn't leave.

Tip: After wish, shift the tense; don't keep ordinary present.

TRUE — If only + were correctly wishes for an unreal present length of break.

Tip: If only + past / were = present counterfactual.

FALSE — A scientific fact belongs in zero conditional, and will expands is doubly wrong (will + -s).

Tip: Zero facts: present + present; never will expands.

TRUE — Clean zero conditional for a physical law.

Tip: Permanent truths keep both clauses in present simple.
highlights: If only the semester break were
tasks.solution_overview: Contrast wish + would with the illegal wish + present, refresh if only + were, and return to zero conditional form for natural facts.

tasks.title: Task 13
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: If she studied abroad next year, she would improve her Spanish dramatically.
If she will study abroad next year, she improves her Spanish dramatically.
Should you need extra towels, the reception desk will help.
Were the path safer, children would use it after dark.
Had we known the gallery was free on Mondays, we would visit yesterday.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Second conditional can mark an unlikely or tentative future plan (studied / would improve).

Tip: Unlikely future → past + would, even with next year.

FALSE — Will in the if-clause plus bare present improves is a broken first-conditional attempt.

Tip: Real future: If she studies… she will improve…

TRUE — Should you need… is a polite inverted first-conditional alternative to If you need…

Tip: Should + subject + V1 ≈ if + present for formal offers.

TRUE — Were the path safer… correctly inverts a second-conditional if-clause.

Tip: Were + subject + complement replaces If + subject + were.

FALSE — Inverted past perfect needs would have visited for a past result, not would visit yesterday.

Tip: Had we known… → would have + V3 for finished past outcomes.
tasks.solution_overview: Raise the bar with unlikely futures, Should/Were inversion, and Had-inversion. Keep will out of if-clauses and keep past results in would have.

tasks.title: Task 14
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: If it had not been for the flat tyre, we would be camping by the lake tonight.
But for the flat tyre, we would be camping by the lake tonight.
If it was not for the flat tyre, we would have arrived hours ago.
As long as nobody objects, we can move the rehearsal to Thursday.
Unless anyone will complain, we can move the rehearsal to Thursday.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Mixed pattern: past obstacle (had not been) with present/future-facing result (would be camping tonight).

Tip: If it had not been for X + would + V1 = past cause, present effect.

TRUE — But for + noun is a compact equivalent of if it were not / had not been for.

Tip: But for X ≈ without X / if not for X.

FALSE — Prefer If it hadn't been for… would have arrived… (past) or If it weren't for… would be… (present); was not for with would have is non-standard here.

Tip: Keep If it weren't for (present) and If it hadn't been for (past) distinct.

TRUE — As long as + present + can correctly sets a real group condition.

Tip: As long as supports present modal results as well as will.

FALSE — Unless + will is wrong; use Unless anyone complains…

Tip: No will after unless in standard condition clauses.
highlights: If it had not been for
tasks.solution_overview: Practise If it had not been for / But for, keep weren't for versus hadn't been for distinct, and strip will from unless.

tasks.title: Task 15
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: I wish I would have more free evenings.
I wish I had more free evenings.
If only the train hadn't been delayed, we wouldn't be queueing now.
If the coach hadn't been delayed, we wouldn't be queueing now.
Supposing the café closed early, where would we study?
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Wish + would have is wrong for a present lack; use wish + past simple (had).

Tip: Wish I would have… is a classic exam error for present wishes.

TRUE — Wish + past simple correctly expresses an unreal present desire.

Tip: Present wish about states → past simple after wish.

TRUE — If only + past perfect cause with wouldn't be now is a valid mixed regret linking past delay to present queue.

Tip: Past perfect after if only can feed a present would/wouldn't result.

TRUE — Same mixed pattern with ordinary if instead of if only.

Tip: Past unreal cause → present continuous-looking result with would/wouldn't + be + -ing.

TRUE — Supposing + past simple introduces a second-conditional hypothesis with would in the question.

Tip: Supposing / suppose ≈ if for tentative scenarios.
tasks.solution_overview: Kill the wish I would have trap, keep wish + past for present states, and confirm mixed past→present with if / if only plus supposing.

tasks.title: Task 16
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Even if the tickets are expensive, we will still go to the festival.
Even if the tickets were free, we will still stay home.
Whether or not it rains, the charity run will start at nine.
If so be the weather improves, we will hike.
If need be, we can share taxis after the concert.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Even if + present + will correctly means the result holds despite the condition.

Tip: Even if ≠ if; the main clause still follows real-future will here.

FALSE — Even if + past (were) wants would stay, not will stay.

Tip: Match even if tense to the result: past → would; present → will.

TRUE — Whether or not + present + will correctly says the run happens regardless of rain.

Tip: Whether or not = no matter if.

FALSE — If so be is archaic and not exam-standard; use If the weather improves…

Tip: Stick to standard if + present for real futures.

TRUE — If need be is an accepted fixed phrase meaning if it is necessary, here with can.

Tip: If need be is a set idiom; don't "correct" it to if needs be in formal keys.
highlights: Even if the tickets were, we will
tasks.solution_overview: Cover even if, whether or not, and fixed if need be, while rejecting tense clashes and archaic if so be.

tasks.title: Task 17
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: If she were to apply for the scholarship, she would need two references.
If she was to have applied last term, she would need two references now.
Were he to practise daily, his serve would improve within weeks.
If I knew then what I know now, I would have chosen a different module.
If I had known then what I know now, I would have chosen a different module.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — If she were to apply is a formal second-conditional way to mark a hypothetical future step.

Tip: If + were to + V1 ≈ unlikely/formal if + past.

FALSE — Was to have applied mixed with would need now is over-stacked and non-standard for this item.

Tip: Prefer clear mixed or third forms; avoid was to have + mismatched results.

TRUE — Were he to practise… correctly inverts were to for a hypothetical training plan.

Tip: Were + subject + to + V1 replaces If + subject + were to.

FALSE — Knew then is underpowered for a clear past knowledge gap; the standard line uses had known then.

Tip: Past counterfactual knowledge → past perfect in the if-clause.

TRUE — Classic form: past perfect for past ignorance, would have chosen for the past decision.

Tip: Had known then… would have + V3 is the polished exam form.
tasks.solution_overview: Advanced were to / Were … to inversion and the had known then pattern. Reject tangled was to have stacks and underpowered knew then for past counterfactuals.

tasks.title: Task 18
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: I'd rather you didn't stream loud videos while I'm revising.
I'd rather you don't stream loud videos while I'm revising.
It's time we left for the airport.
It's time we leave for the airport.
Suppose you won free concert tickets — what would you do?
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Would rather + past simple correctly softens a present preference about someone else's behaviour (conditional-adjacent).

Tip: I'd rather you + past = polite present preference.

FALSE — After I'd rather you, use past simple, not present don't.

Tip: Same backshift habit as wish: prefer past after I'd rather you.

TRUE — It's time + past simple is the standard formal pattern for a present urgency.

Tip: It's time we left = we should leave now.

FALSE — Careful exam keys usually want It's time we left, not leave.

Tip: It's time + past is the marked formal choice.

TRUE — Suppose + past + would correctly frames a second-conditional daydream.

Tip: Suppose / supposing pattern like if + past.
tasks.solution_overview: Extend conditional logic into I'd rather you, it's time + past, and suppose. These share the same backshift instinct as wish and second conditionals.

tasks.title: Task 19
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: If the inflation rate drops, household budgets will feel less pressure next quarter.
Had the storm not hit, the outdoor market would still be open this afternoon.
If only I could have attended the reunion last month.
I wish I could have attended the reunion last month.
Unless having finished the essay, she will not join us.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — First conditional with a real possible macro change and a future lifestyle effect.

Tip: Real future → present + will.

TRUE — Mixed: past unreal storm (Had … not hit) with present result (would still be open).

Tip: Negative inversion Had … not + V3 can feed a present would result.

TRUE — If only + could have + V3 correctly regrets a missed past ability/opportunity.

Tip: If only I could have… = past inability regret.

TRUE — Wish + could have + V3 matches the same past missed opportunity.

Tip: Wish I could have… parallels if only for past regrets about ability.

FALSE — Unless needs a finite clause (Unless she has finished…), not Unless having finished…

Tip: Unless + subject + verb; avoid dangling -ing after unless.
tasks.solution_overview: Combine one light economy first conditional, mixed Had-not inversion, wish / if only + could have, and reject non-finite unless having.

tasks.title: Task 20
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: It's high time we booked the campsite.
If you come to the hike, bring a reusable bottle.
I'll come cycling with you on Sunday provided the weather holds.
I'll come cycling with you on Sunday provided the weather will hold.
No sooner had we sat down than the fire alarm would go off.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — It's high time + past simple correctly marks present urgency with the same backshift as wish / it's time.

Tip: It's (high) time + past = we should do it now.

TRUE — Clear first-conditional imperative result: if + present, imperative bring…

Tip: Imperatives are fine as first-conditional results.

TRUE — Provided + present (holds) correctly sets a real weather condition for a future plan with will come.

Tip: Provided / providing + present, not will.

FALSE — Provided the weather will hold wrongly inserts will into the condition.

Tip: Same rule as if / as long as: no will in the proviso clause.

FALSE — No sooner… than needs a simple past result (went off), not conditional would go off.

Tip: No sooner is past sequencing, not a conditional frame.
highlights: If you come to the hike, bring
tasks.solution_overview: Finish with it's high time, imperative first conditionals, and provided + present, while rejecting will after provided and would forced onto a no sooner sequence.
